To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

feeding pattern can influence body composition and adipocyte cellularity, and that cafeteria feeding can induce obesity in mice of the polygenic obese strain, C57L/J, but not in the control normal strain, C57BR/cdJ.

the cafeteria diet and the restriction of food intake to a level that produces 70% of ad libitum intake both produce obesity and that the increase in fat content in the obese mice on the cafeteria diet is due to genetic effects, while the increase in fat in the obese mice fed the restricted diets is due mainly to the effect of acute restriction of food intake.

the effects of varying feed intake during the early post-weaning period on growth of polygenic obese mice are due to genetic effects, while the increase in the percentage of fat after restriction on the MI, PM and PM treatments is due mainly to the effect of acute changes in the feeding pattern.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of diet and feeding pattern on body composition in the early postweanling period in polygenic obese mouse lines.
the effect of varying feed intakes and feeding patterns on body composition and adipocyte size and number.
the development of obesity and the effects of feeding pattern on growth and adiposity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
feeding pattern is an important factor in determining body composition in both obese and nonobese mice, but that this is not the only factor involved.
the effects of feeding pattern on growth, body weight, body composition and fat cell size are dependent upon genetic background and dietary regimen.
the effects of feeding pattern on growth, body weight, body composition and fat pad cellularity are influenced by genetic background.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a genetic predisposition to obesity is not expressed in the absence of an environmental stimulus.
obesity in mice is influenced by genetic factors and the pattern of feeding.
the cafeteria-fed obese mouse is a model for genetic obesity and that the obese mouse on restricted diet is a model for the effects of dietary manipulation on body composition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cafeteria diet is not an ideal diet for inducing obesity in mice.
the development of obesity is a complex process involving genetic, physiological and behavioral factors.
the effects of dietary regimen on adipose tissue cell size are not due to the amount of food ingested but to the pattern of feeding.
